title: Postoperative Respiratory Care (Abdominal and Thoracic Surgery)

blocks.text: After major surgery, especially upper abdominal and thoracic surgery, anaesthesia, pain, opioids, immobility and reduced diaphragm function lower lung volumes. This can cause atelectasis, sputum retention, and postoperative pulmonary complications (PPCs) such as pneumonia. Risk factors include upper abdominal or thoracic incision, older age, smoking, COPD, obesity, long surgery, and poor pre-operative fitness [Ref – to verify].

blocks.label: WHY THIS MATTERS
body: Pre-operative education and early mobilisation have shown reduced pulmonary complications after major abdominal surgery in some trials [Ref – to verify LIPPSMAck-POP]. Physiotherapy starts before the operation.

sections.title: B to C. Assessment questions and review

blocks.text: Type of surgery and incision; analgesia (epidural, patient-controlled); drains, lines, catheters; surgical restrictions; pre-operative mobility; smoking; lung disease; pain level.
Vital signs, oxygen requirement, pain score, auscultation, cough effectiveness (with wound support), bed mobility, sitting and standing ability, calf check.

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Rising RR, fever, new crackles or bronchial breathing
Low BP, high HR, increased drain output or wound bleeding
Air leak increasing, subcutaneous emphysema, sudden breathlessness with chest drain
Medical team; do not clamp drains

steps: **Pre-operative:** educate about breathing exercises, supported cough, early mobilisation; encourage fitness and smoking cessation.
**Day 0 to 1 post-op:** check stability; sit out of bed and walk if able, with drains managed safely.
**Signs of atelectasis or sputum?** Add deep breathing, ACBT, supported cough, positioning.

rows: Sit out, stand, walk with lines and drains secured
Several times daily from day 1 if stable
5 to 10 breaths every hour while awake
Hold a pillow or folded towel firmly over the incision; huff then cough
Use as an adjunct; evidence for routine use alone is limited [Ref – to verify]
Active range on the operated side

blocks.text: Chest drains: keep the drainage bottle below chest level, never lift above the patient, do not clamp unless instructed, watch for swinging and bubbling as instructed.
SpO2 and oxygen need, auscultation, temperature trend, walking distance, pain-limited breathing.

items: **Why are upper abdominal operations high risk?** Pain and diaphragm dysfunction reduce lung volumes.
**What is the single most important postoperative intervention?** Early mobilisation.
**Why support the wound during cough?** Reduces pain and allows a stronger cough.
**Where should a chest drain bottle be kept?** Below the level of the chest.
**When does physiotherapy start for planned major surgery?** Before surgery, with education and fitness.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Identify patients at high risk of PPCs.
Mobilise early safely with lines and drains.
